readerTitle: Why Quaker's winning drinks playbook failed with Snapple
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Quaker Oats의 Snapple 인수) + Berkshire Hathaway 주주서한의 개념 + 가상 적용 (식품 제조사, 치과용 소프트웨어)
insight: 능력의 범위는 크기보다 경계가 중요하다. 가장 위험한 곳은 먼 분야가 아니라 비슷해 보이지만 돈을 버는 방식이 다른 옆 분야다.
misconception: 한 분야에서 크게 성공했으면 비슷한 제품이나 시장도 잘 안다.

sources.text: Buffett, W. (1996). Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder Letter (circle of competence)
Quaker Oats acquisition of Snapple (1994) and sale to Triarc (1997), contemporary press coverage, e.g. The New York Times

factChecks.note: Quaker의 Snapple 인수 금액(약 17억 달러, 1994년)과 매각 금액(약 3억 달러, 1997년 Triarc)은 당시 보도 기준입니다. 게시 전 1차 보도로 다시 확인하세요.
Quaker가 Snapple 유통을 Gatorade식 대형 유통망으로 바꾸려다 독립 유통업자들의 반발을 산 내용은 여러 사례 분석에 나옵니다. 카드에는 세부 수치 없이 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
Buffett 인용문("The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.")은 1996년 주주서한 원문과 대조하세요.

cards.title: Why Quaker's winning drinks playbook failed with Snapple
body: In the early 1990s, Quaker Oats had turned Gatorade into a giant. It knew how to sell drinks.
So in 1994 it bought Snapple, a fast-growing iced tea brand, for about $1.7 billion. Three years later it sold Snapple for about $300 million.

image.label: Two drink bottles on diverging delivery routes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두 종류의 음료병이 갈림길에 서 있음. 한쪽 길은 대형 마트 창고로, 다른 쪽 길은 작은 동네 가게와 소형 트럭으로 이어짐. 실제 브랜드 로고와 라벨 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A drink that looks just like yours.
body: You run a food manufacturer. Your sports drink sells hugely through supermarkets. You can buy a hot iced-tea brand. It sells mostly cold, one bottle at a time, in corner shops and gas stations, delivered by small independent distributors.
What do you do?

options.text: Buy it and move it into your supermarket system to cut costs
options.feedback: You gain scale and savings on paper. But you might break the distribution that made the brand grow, in a channel you don't know well.

options.text: Before deciding, list what you'd have to learn about this channel, and price that in
options.feedback: It costs time and may kill the deal. It also shows you whether this business is really similar to yours, or only looks similar.

options.text: Pass. Never buy outside your main product
options.feedback: Safe, but it may skip a good deal. The question isn't whether it's new. It's whether you know where your knowledge stops.

cards.title: Same shelf, different business.
body: Gatorade moved in large loads to supermarket warehouses. Snapple grew through independent distributors who stocked small shops and coolers bottle by bottle.
Quaker tried to bring Snapple into its own system. Distributors pushed back, and the brand's sales slid. Quaker knew **drinks**, but not this way of selling them.
The product looked like home. The engine behind it did not.

cards.title: Circle of competence
body: Your **circle of competence** is the set of areas where you truly understand how things work: how money is made, what usually goes wrong, and why.
Warren Buffett put it this way in his 1996 letter: "The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."
Quaker's circle was real. Its mistake was drawing the boundary too wide.

image.label: A circle with a solid core and a blurry edge
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 진한 원 안쪽에 "I can explain it", 흐릿한 가장자리에 "Looks familiar", 바깥에 "I don't know". 가장자리 띠를 경고색으로 강조.

cards.title: Three questions mark the edge.
body: Inside your circle, you can answer these without guessing:
list: **How does it make money?** Explain it in two sentences.
**What usually kills it?** Name the common ways it fails.
**Who would beat you, and why?** Know the people who do this every day.
cards.callout: If an answer starts with "probably," you're at the edge.

cards.title: The danger is next door, not far away.
body: Nobody at a bakery thinks they can run a shipping line. Distant fields feel risky, so people are careful.
Neighboring fields feel safe. A bakery opening a wholesale line, or a parts maker starting its own trucking fleet, sees familiar products and misses the different engine.
You can still step out. Do it on purpose: start small, hire people who already live there, and expect to be slower at first.

cards.title: The circle is not a cage.
body: Used badly, this idea becomes an excuse to never grow. Every circle was once outside someone's circle.
Circles also shrink. Customers, technology and rules change, and what you knew ten years ago may no longer hold.
And most people rate their own circle as larger than it is. Ask someone outside your team to test the boundary.

cards.title: Now it's software for dental clinics.
body: Your scheduling software is loved by dental clinics. Customers ask you to handle patient payments too, which could double revenue per clinic.
Your team has never run payments, fraud checks or billing rules. What do you do?

options.text: Build your own payment processing in-house
options.feedback: You'd keep all the revenue, but payments has its own failure modes, like fraud and compliance, where one mistake can hurt every clinic.

options.text: Partner with a payment provider and own the clinic experience
options.feedback: You give up some revenue but stay inside what you know: clinics and their workflow. You learn the new area with far less risk.

options.text: Ignore the request and stay in scheduling
options.feedback: Safe today, but a rival who adds payments may take your customers. Staying inside the circle shouldn't mean ignoring its edge.

cards.title: Know where your knowledge stops.
body: What looks like your business may run on a different engine. The edge of your circle matters more than its size.
**Try it today:** take your next big idea and answer the three questions in writing. Circle every answer that starts with "probably."
